entries.t: FlexSpace gives you a canvas: an editor where you lay out your own buttons, sliders, toggles, labels and images, then use them while you work. Run operators and scripts, drive any property, keep your tools one click away. It comes with two canvases: Flex Space, for control panels, and Armature Picker, a canvas of buttons that select the bones of your rig so you can pose without hunting for them in the viewport.

In any area, open the Editor Type menu (the first button of the header) and pick Flex Space. Click New in the header (or the New button of the card in the middle). Note: The canvas is a data-block saved in your .blend file, like a material or a node group. Pick, rename or make one from the selector in the middle of the header.

Every canvas has two modes. Press Tab over the canvas (or click Edit in the header) to switch. Edit Mode: build the layout. Add, move, resize, rotate, group and style widgets. Live Mode: use the widgets. Click buttons, drag sliders, flip toggles. Press Tab for Edit Mode. Press Shift A and choose a widget, for example Data > Numbers > Lineal (or just type lineal). Click to place it. Open the sidebar (N), Widget tab, and set what it controls. For a slider, type a Data Path such as scene.frame_current, or use the eyedropper button next to the field and right-click any property in Blender. Tip: Faster: Shift A > From Property, then right-click any property in Blender. The right widget is added, already bound (see Widgets > Add from Property). Tip: From anywhere in Blender: right-click a property or a button and choose Add to FlexSpace Canvas, then a canvas and page (see Binding Properties > Add to FlexSpace Canvas).
Press Tab to go back to Live Mode and drag the slider. Every widget and what it can drive: Widgets, Color & Brush Widgets and Binding Properties.

Select your rig, enter Pose Mode (Ctrl Tab in the 3D Viewport), and in another area pick Armature Picker from the Editor Type menu. Click New Picker on the card, select some bones in the 3D Viewport and click Import Selected Bones. Click to place each button (the left and right bones of a pair come together). Press Tab to go back to posing and click a button: its bone is selected. Note: The picker is saved with the armature data, so it travels with the rig, also when you link or append it. It can hold sliders, toggles and pads too: a knob for the jaw, a pad for the eyes, a switch for IK and FK. More in The Armature Picker and Picker with Rigify.

Header: Edit toggle, the View, Selection (Edit Mode) and Help menus, canvas selector, presets, snapping, minimap, pages and widget visibility. Help holds this guide, the demo files and Report a Bug.... Sidebar (N): the Widget tab holds the active widget's settings. The Canvas tab holds the pages and their modes, and the Library of canvases and global presets. A picker adds an Armature tab (bone names, bone collections). Picker header: Utils (import bones, repair bindings). The Toolbar (T) sets what a press on a button does: select, move, rotate or scale its bone. Right-click in Edit Mode: the context menu (grouping, frames, order, delete). Preferences > Add-ons > FlexSpace: modules, themes and add-on settings.

Demo Files: open a finished control panel in a new window (Help > Demo Files, or Open a Demo on the card of an empty editor) and see how it is made. Recipes: set up a full studio for Sculpt, Texture Paint, Weight Paint or Grease Pencil, step by step. The Canvas: move around, use pages and set up the add-on. Shortcuts: all the keys.

FlexSpace has two kinds of canvas, each with its own editor: Flex Space: a blank board for your own control panel. Put operator buttons, scripts, sliders, toggles, labels and images on it, then use them from any workspace. Armature Picker: a canvas saved with an armature, for picking its bones while you pose. Posing and bones are on The Armature Picker page. Both work the same way. This page covers what they share.

Set an area to Flex Space (Editor Type menu). Click New. Each canvas is saved in the .blend file. The selector in the header switches between canvases, renames them and adds a fake user. To use a canvas from another file, bring it in with File > Link or File > Append (it is under NodeTree). The file keeps it, even if no editor shows it: A linked canvas stays in the other file and updates when that file changes. The scene keeps a reference to it. To remove it, delete it in the Outliner's Blender File view. An appended canvas is a copy you can edit. It gets a fake user.

A canvas has two modes. Tab switches between them. Edit Mode is for building: Shift A adds a widget, drag to move it, use the handles around the selection to resize or rotate it. Live Mode is for using: buttons run, toggles switch, sliders change their property. Rest the mouse on a widget for a tooltip: what it does or the property it drives (see Widgets > Tooltips). On an Armature Picker, Live Mode is Blender's own Pose Mode: you use the picker while you pose, so the picker calls it Pose Mode. A canvas linked from another file (File > Link) is always in Live Mode, even if its file was saved in Edit Mode. Edit its layout in the file it comes from. Tip: The pill at the bottom of the canvas reminds you of Tab. Turn it off with Key Hints in the add-on preferences.

Middle mouse drag pans. Ctrl Middle mouse drag zooms. The Wheel zooms. It follows Blender's Invert Zoom Wheel preference. Ctrl Wheel scrolls sideways, Shift Wheel up and down. A trackpad pans and pinches to zoom. Numpad + and Numpad - zoom too. Home frames every widget. The minimap (header, picture icon) shows the whole canvas: click to centre, drag to pan. Navigation is Blender's own, as in the Node Editor: it follows your View2D keymap, whatever button you bound. Industry Compatible (Alt with the middle or left mouse pans, Alt right mouse zooms), Emulate 3 Button Mouse and your own bindings work. A binding on a plain left or right click navigates instead of selecting, as it does in the Node Editor; an edit handle, a widget in Live Mode or a page tab under the mouse still takes the left click, but not an Alt click, so Industry Compatible pans over picker buttons too. Bind it to Click Drag to keep the click for selecting. A right mouse binding takes over the picker's keyframe pie, and a right mouse Click Drag binding works on a canvas even though the Node Editor's context menu would open first there. A 3D mouse (NDOF) doesn't navigate a canvas. In Live Mode, a widget that uses the wheel keeps it: a List scrolls its rows, with the wheel or a two-finger trackpad scroll. Note: With natural scrolling on, Ctrl with a two-finger trackpad scroll may zoom the other way from Blender's own editors. A pinch zooms the same way.

A canvas can have several pages, each with its own widgets. Each page can also be made for one Blender mode, for example Sculpt Mode or Weight Paint, or for one object of the scene. So one canvas can hold a sculpting page full of brushes, a weight paint page, the controls of one object and an everyday page, and show the right one for what you are doing. Pick the active page in the header, or click its tab at the top-left of the canvas in Live Mode (the tabs show when two or more pages are pinned). In a narrow editor the tabs squeeze to fit: object names go first, then long page names are shortened with an ellipsis. When even that doesn't fit, the tabs hide, and the page menu in the header still switches pages. Add a page with the + button next to it. In Edit Mode, M moves the selected widgets to another page. The dialog starts on the first other page. A widget leaves its frame, unless the frame moves too: a moved frame takes its widgets along. The Pages panel in the Canvas tab of the sidebar (N) lists the pages. The icon at the right of each one sets its mode. Show When below the list sets when the active page fits. The buttons next to the list add, remove and duplicate the active page. A duplicate copies the page's widgets, with their frames, groups and Flex Boxes, and the page's settings: its mode, Show When and tab. An empty page can be duplicated too. Show When has four choices: Always, the default: the page works everywhere. Mode: the page is for one Blender mode, set in Mode below it. Object: the page is for one object, set in Object below it. It fits while that object is the active one, in any mode. Pick the object in the field, with its eyedropper, or click Use Active for the active object. Object in Mode: both. For example, a tower's Geometry Nodes controls that only show while the tower is active in Object Mode. A page made for a mode shows that mode's icon on its tab and in the header. A page made for an object shows the object's icon and name on its tab, after the page name. What you see: A thin border in the mode's colour shows the active page's mode at a glance. A tab whose page doesn't fit right now (another mode, or another active object) is dimmed. You can still click it. When the active page needs another mode, the canvas is dimmed and its widgets don't react. A notice says which mode it needs. Click Enter on the notice to switch to that mode, when the active object can, or click another tab. When the active page is for an object that isn't the active one, the notice says This page is for that object. Click Select on it: the object becomes active and selected (shown again if you hid it with H), in the page's mode for Object in Mode. If the page's object was deleted, or isn't in this file, the notice says it is missing. Click Use on it to use the active object instead. Switch Pages Automatically (in the Pages panel, on by default) shows the right page for you. When Blender's mode or the active object changes, the canvas shows the page that fits best. Object in Mode comes first, then Object, then Mode, then Always. When two pages fit just as well, the first tab wins, and a tab you clicked yourself stays while it still fits as well. With no page that fits, nothing changes. It waits while you edit the layout or drag a widget. Undo and redo count too: when Ctrl Z brings back another mode or active object, the canvas shows the page that fits it. Note: The canvas's Edit Mode (Tab) still works in any Blender mode, so you can build a page's layout first. A button can change the mode too: an Operator button that runs Enter Mode makes an object active and selected (and shows it if you hid it with H), frames it in the 3D Viewport if you like, and enters a mode with it. The FlexSpace Studio demo has one for each mode (see Recipes). Some widgets need a mode of their own: The Add menu greys out the widgets that don't fit the active page's mode. Hover one to see why. On an Any Mode page, these widgets draw a small warning mark when Blender is in another mode. Note: Changing a page's mode never deletes widgets. A warning tells you how many don't fit. An Armature Picker's pages always work in Pose Mode. Their mode is not shown and can't be changed. Note: Files from earlier versions set one mode for the whole canvas. When the file opens, that mode moves to each of its pages that was set to Any Mode. Pages saved with a mode, before Show When, read as Mode. Tip: A global preset remembers each page's object by name. Added to another file, the page finds the object of that name there. If there is none, the notice says which object is missing.
The last menu of the header (View Object Types) hides or shows each widget type in this editor. Tip: Hide the buttons to work on sliders without them in the way.

Canvas keys come first. Any key the canvas does not use goes on to Blender, as set in your keymap: Space plays the animation. Ctrl Space maximizes the area. Ctrl S saves. Ctrl Z undoes. Industry Compatible and custom bindings work too.

In Edit Mode, a thin bar runs across the top of the canvas. It shows, from left to right: the global preset of the canvas (see below), or Local canvas; its state and the actions that apply; on an armature picker, the armature and how many of the picker's bones it has, for example Rig 142/142 bones; at the right end, the bindings that need you, on every page that works in the current mode and with the active object (shown widget types only): ⚠ 2 broken (a path that leads nowhere or to the wrong kind of property, a missing operator) and a muted 1 unbound (bound to nothing yet). With nothing broken or unbound, it doesn't show. Click the binding count to go to the next broken widget: it is selected, its page is shown if it was on another one, the view frames it, and the sidebar opens on its Widget tab, where the note under its field says what is wrong. Click again for the next one. With nothing broken, a click goes through the unbound widgets instead. The minimap, the Selection Bar and Home stay below the bar, so it never covers them. Hover an item for a tooltip. In Live Mode there is no bar. A pill shows in the top-right corner only when the preset needs you: a newer version is available, or the preset is missing. Click it for the preset menu. With nothing to report, nothing shows.

A global preset is a canvas saved outside the .blend file, so every project can use it. Presets are kept in the add-on's user folder and survive add-on updates. The preset button next to the canvas selector opens the presets menu. To save a canvas as a global preset: Show the canvas in Edit Mode. Click Save as Global... on the top bar (or Save as Global Preset... in the presets menu). Name it and click Save. To use a preset in another project, open the presets menu and click its name. The menu shows each preset as a thumbnail. Presets with a page for Blender's current mode come first. A thumbnail is made each time you save or overwrite the preset. A canvas added this way is linked to the preset. It remembers which version of the preset it came from. Your edits stay in this file until you choose to send them to the preset. The top bar shows the preset's name with a link icon, then its state: Badge Meaning ✓ Up to date Same as the preset. ● Modified You changed the canvas. The preset is unchanged. ↓ vN available Another project overwrote the preset: version N is newer. ● Modified and ↓ vN available Both changed. ⚠ Missing The preset's files are not on this computer. ⚠ Unavailable A newer Blender saved the preset, or its canvas type is not available. The buttons after the badge show only when they apply: Overwrite (↑, when you changed the canvas) sends your canvas to the preset. Other projects get it when they update. If another project changed the preset since your version, Blender asks first. Sync (↓, when either side changed) replaces your canvas with the preset. If you changed the canvas, Blender asks first, because your changes will be lost. Unlink keeps the canvas as a plain copy in this file. Click the preset's name for the preset menu. It has the same actions, plus Restore Previous Version: the last 5 versions that Overwrite replaced. The one you pick becomes the preset's new version. Blender asks first. The presets menu also opens it, as This Canvas' Preset. When a file opens, linked canvases you have not changed get the preset's newer version. Canvases you changed are never updated by themselves. To turn this off, clear Update Unmodified Presets in the add-on preferences. A linked canvas whose preset is not on this computer keeps working from its own copy. The top bar shows ⚠ Missing, with Restore... (save it back as the preset) and Unlink. To rename or delete a preset, use Manage in the presets menu. Both ask you to confirm. Projects that use a deleted preset keep their canvas.

To move a preset to another computer, or to send it to someone, export it as one file: Open the presets menu, then Manage > Export. Click the preset and pick where to save it. The file ends in .flexspace. It holds the preset's current version and its thumbnail. To add a preset from a file, use Manage > Import... and pick the .flexspace file. The preset keeps its identity, so canvases that were linked to it in other files find it again. If you already have this preset, If It Exists (in the file browser's side panel) decides what happens: Add a Copy (default): the preset is added as a new one, with a number after its name. Replace: the file's version replaces yours. Your old version is kept in Restore Previous Version, and linked canvases see it as an update. Replace changes the preset where it is. If that preset is in the shared folder, it changes for everyone, whatever Into says. The preset also takes the name it has in the file, so a preset you renamed gets its old name back. Import checks the file first. A damaged file, a file with anything else inside, or a preset saved by a newer Blender is refused with a message, and nothing is added.

A team can share presets from one folder, for example on a network drive. Set Shared Presets Folder in the add-on preferences (Addon Settings, under Global Presets). The presets in that folder are listed with yours, and you add them the same way. In the Library panel, a shared preset shows a network-drive icon. If the folder can't be written, it shows a lock instead. The presets menu adds (Shared) to their names. If you can write to the folder, Overwrite, rename and delete work on shared presets too. They change the preset for everyone. If the folder is read-only, you can add and export its presets, but not change them. To put a preset in the shared folder, export it, then import it with Into: Shared Folder. This option shows when a shared folder is set. You can also copy preset folders there. Note: If you have a preset with the same identity as one in the shared folder, your own copy is the one used. FlexSpace reads the shared folder in the background, every few seconds, so a slow or offline network drive never freezes Blender. A preset a teammate adds shows up after a moment. While the folder can't be reached, its presets are not listed, and canvases linked to them show as missing. Note: While the shared folder can't be reached, Restore Global Preset is refused for a missing preset, because it may be in that folder. A copy saved on your computer would hide the shared one. Reconnect the folder, or unlink the canvas and save it as a new preset. Tip: Picker presets find their bones by name. On another rig with the same bone names, the picker works right away. The presets menu shows how many of the preset's bones the active armature has.

The Library panel, under Pages in the Canvas tab of the sidebar (N), lists the canvases of this editor's type: Global: every global preset, whether this file uses it or not. Click one to add it, or to show it if the file already has it. A linked preset shows a badge when it is modified or has an update. Local: the canvases in this file that are not linked to a preset. Click one to show it. The canvas shown in the editor is highlighted.

A canvas copied whole keeps its pages, frames, groups and Flex Boxes as they are. This covers the number button next to its name (make it single user), Duplicate in the Outliner, and File > Append from another file. The copy is independent: changing it never changes the original, and the same preset or template can be added several times.

Every edit and every use of a widget is one undo step: a move, a slider drag, a toggle click. Adding, removing or duplicating a page and moving widgets to another page are one step each too. Switching between Edit Mode and Live Mode is not a step, and undo never switches it back: undo a slider drag in Live Mode and you stay in Live Mode. Clicking a page tab is not a step either. Undo and redo keep the page you are looking at, as they keep the view. The page of the step shows only when the step itself adds or removes pages or moves widgets to another page, and Switch Pages Automatically still follows a mode or active object that undo brings back.

Edit > Preferences > Add-ons > FlexSpace has four sections, listed on the left: Modules: the built-in modules, with the defaults of their widgets. Themes: the colours, shape and type of the widgets. Make your own theme here. Demo Files: example files to open in a new window (see Demo Files). Addon Settings: Appearance (Auto, Dark, Light), widget animations, Key Hints, where the Selection Bar shows, Update Unmodified Presets, the Shared Presets Folder, and the theme library folder.

Widget What it does Modes Example Operator Runs a Blender operator All Custom Script Runs your own Python script All Toggle Switches an on / off property, or sets an enum or integer value All Enum Picks one value of an enum or integer All Color Swatch Shows a colour and opens Blender's colour picker All Color Picker Edits a colour on the canvas (see Color & Brush Widgets) All Color Palette A grid of colour swatches (see Color & Brush Widgets) All Brush Picker Makes one brush the active brush (see Color & Brush Widgets) Brush modes Ring Menu Brushes, toggles and operators in a ring, like a sculpt wheel (see Color & Brush Widgets) All List Shows layers, material slots, vertex groups and other lists as rows you can click All Lineal slider Drag along a bar to change a number All Number Field A number field like Blender's own All Label Text, or a property's value All Image Shows a picture All View Preview A live 3D view: objects, a camera or a viewport All — Frame A titled area, square or round, that holds and moves other widgets All Flex Box Lines up other widgets in a row or a column All Group Moves and resizes other widgets as one All The picker adds a few widgets of its own: Widget What it does Modes Example Bone Collection toggle Shows, hides or solos a bone collection All Radial slider A knob you drag to change a number All Lineal 2D slider A pad that drives two properties at once All Button, Button Image, Geometry Shape Bone pickers: select their bone All How to add and set up a widget: In Edit Mode, press Shift A and pick a widget (see The Add menu below), or use the header's Add menu. Select it and open the sidebar (N), Widget tab. Set its Label: Auto (the name of the bound property; for a node input, the input's name, such as Roughness), Custom (your text) or None. Change its look in the Style panel (see Editing Tools > Themes). Optional: in the Conditions panel, show it only while a property is on (Visible When) or grey it out (Disabled When). See Binding Properties > Show, hide or disable a widget with a property. Note: Most widgets have the Label and Style settings, not all of them.

In Live Mode, rest the mouse on a widget for a moment and a tooltip tells what it does: an Operator button: the operator's name and description. When it can't run right now, the tooltip says Can't run here, and why when the operator tells (for example No active object). With Blender's Python Tooltips on, it also shows the operator's Python name. a Custom Script button: the script it runs. a widget bound to a property (Toggle, sliders, Number Field, Enum, colour widgets, List, a Label showing a value): the property's name and description, and its data path, muted. A problem with the binding (a path that leads nowhere, a read-only property, a property of the wrong kind) shows in the warning colour, as on the widget. a Brush Picker: the brush's name. a View Preview: what it shows (its target, its camera and resolution, or the viewport it follows) and, when you can orbit it, how. An Operator or Custom Script button from an untrusted file also says that a click asks before running it. Other widgets (Frame, Flex Box, Image, a text Label, bone pickers) have no tooltip of their own. To write your own for any widget, select it in Edit Mode and type it in the sidebar, Widget tab, Tooltip panel. Your text replaces the description; the name, the data path and any warning stay. A Label or an Image with a tooltip of yours shows it too, and clicks still go through them; over a widget that takes the click, that widget's tooltip shows instead, since it tells what the click does. A long text is cut short, so keep it to a sentence or two. As in Blender, the tooltip waits until the mouse rests; moving the mouse hides it and resting again brings it back. It hides when the mouse leaves the widget or the canvas, on a click or a key (Shift, Ctrl or Alt alone keep it), and in Edit Mode. It follows Blender's Preferences > Interface > Tooltips: off there, no widget tooltips either. The Ring Menu has none: it names its items itself.

Shift A opens the Add Widget panel over the canvas: Search: just start typing, no click needed. The best match is selected, and Enter adds it. Categories: the column on the left. Tab goes to the next one. Buttons: Operator, Custom Script. Data: widgets that show or edit a property, in subcategories: Toggles, Choices, Numbers, Color, Text, Lists. Click Data to see them all under headings, or a subcategory for just those. Tools: Brush Picker, Ring Menu. Graphics: Image, Backdrop Image, and the 3D Views: View Preview, Camera View, Viewport Mirror, Silhouette. Layout: Flex Boxes, Frame. In an armature picker, Bone Picker comes first. From Property has its own button next to the search: pick a property in Blender and get the right widget for it. Cards: click one to add it. The new widget follows the mouse; click to place it. The arrow keys move the selection. A widget the page's mode can't take is dimmed, and the bottom of the panel says why. Esc, a right-click or a click outside closes it. The editor's header has an Add menu with Search... (the panel), From Property... and the same categories, the subcategories under headings. From Live Mode it switches to Edit Mode first. Tip: Prefer the pie? In the add-on preferences, set Add Menu to Pie.

The quickest way to add a control: Press Shift A > From Property. Right-click any property in Blender's interface (the Properties editor, the sidebar, a node...). The widget that controls it appears where you opened the menu, already bound and labelled. Blender's menu for that property stays open: move away or press Esc to close it. Esc before picking cancels. Undo removes the whole addition in one step. What you get: Property Widget On / off Toggle (Checkbox) Enum Enum (Segmented with 5 items or less, else Dropdown) Number Number Field Number with a 0–1 style range (Factor or Percentage, with a soft minimum and maximum) Lineal slider with that range Colour Color Swatch Vector (Location, Rotation, Scale... 2 to 4 values) Vertical Flex Box with one Number Field per value Anything else (a name, a data-block, a flag enum, a matrix) Label that reads the value out Custom properties work too: their subtype and soft range decide, as above. Right-clicking one item of a vector adds the whole vector. A property the canvas can't reach is reported, and you can pick another one. Tip: Already in the Properties editor? Right-click the property and choose Add to FlexSpace Canvas: the same widget goes to the canvas and page you pick, without opening the canvas (see Binding Properties > Add to FlexSpace Canvas). Note: In the picker, From Property is also in the header's Utils menu (the widget goes to the middle of the view). Pose-bone properties work as any other. A vector becomes a Group of Number Fields, because the picker has no Flex Box.
Buttons can show a text, an image (Use Image), or both. Fit To Text sizes the button to its label.

Runs a Blender operator, like a button of Blender's own interface. Pick Operator from UI: click it, then right-click any button in Blender. Its operator and settings are copied. Or type it: Context and Action are the two parts of the operator name (pose and select_all for pose.select_all). Operator Properties: the settings it runs with. The button runs as if you clicked in the 3D Viewport. Like Blender's own buttons, a click adds one undo step named after the operator, when the operator can be undone. Tip: The button turns red when its operator can't run right now, for example a pose tool with no armature in Pose Mode.

Runs a Python script of your own. Click Create Script (later Open Script) to write it in a Text Editor window. The script can use active_object, active_widget and canvas. With an armature active, it can also use armature and pose. Each run is one undo step, named after the button's label. Note: A script (and an operator that can run code) is code stored in the .blend file. If Blender's Auto Run Python Scripts is off for this file, the first click asks Run Untrusted Code? before running it. Changing the script asks again.

A Toggle switches an on / off property. Its Data Path must point to a boolean (for example space_data.overlay.show_overlays). Three looks, in the Add menu and in its Shape setting: Radial, Switch and Checkbox. A click is one undo step, keyed if Auto Keying is on.

Set the toggle's Mode to Set Value (or pick Set Value in the Add menu) to drive an enum or an integer instead. Pick the item (or type the number) in Value. Until you pick one, it is the property's first item. The toggle is on while the property has that value, and a click sets it. A click is one undo step, keyed if Auto Keying is on. With Label on Auto, the toggle shows the item's name. Tip: Put a few Set Value toggles side by side to get radio buttons: one per IK / FK value, or one per parent of a space switch.
A toggle bound to a bone collection of the rig. The Add menu asks for the collection. In the sidebar Bone Collection panel choose Visible (show / hide it) or Solo.

An Enum picks one value of a property: a mode, IK / FK, a space or parent switch. Its Data Path points to: an enum property (for example active_object.rotation_mode), or an integer, custom properties too (for example a Rigify parent switch, active_object.pose.bones["hand_ik.L"]["IK_parent"]). What it shows: An enum shows the items of the property, with their names (and their icons in the dropdown list). An integer needs a list of Items in the sidebar: each one is a Value and the Label shown for it. Add Item adds the next value. From Range makes one item per value between the property's minimum and maximum. Without items, a small range shows its numbers. Display (the Add menu has both looks): Segmented: every item side by side, the current one highlighted. Click an item to set it. Orientation stacks them in a column (Vertical). Dropdown: the current item. Click it to open the list and choose. Auto: segmented with 5 items or less, else a dropdown. A change is one undo step, and it is keyed if Blender's Auto Keying is on.

A Color Swatch shows a colour and opens Blender's colour picker for it. Its Data Path points to a colour property, for example: a material's Base Color: active_object.active_material.node_tree.nodes["Principled BSDF"].inputs[0].default_value a material's viewport colour: active_object.active_material.diffuse_color a light: active_object.data.color, the world: scene.world.color an object's viewport display colour: active_object.color Tip: The eyedropper takes any colour field: right-click it in the Properties editor, a node, the sidebar... The swatch shows the colour the way Blender's own colour fields do. A colour with transparency shows the solid colour on its left half and the colour over a checkerboard on its right half. Click it in Live Mode to open the colour picker. Changes made there are Blender's own, so Ctrl Z undoes them as usual. If Auto Keying is on, the colour is keyed when the picker closes.

A List shows a Blender list as rows, like the lists in the Properties editor. Click a row to make it the active item. Pick the list in Source: Source Shows Row toggles Grease Pencil Layers The layers of the active Grease Pencil object, top layer first Hide, Lock Material Slots The material slots of the active object None UV Maps The UV maps of the active mesh Active Render Color Attributes The color attributes of the active mesh None Shape Keys The shape keys of the active object Mute Vertex Groups The vertex groups of the active object Lock Bone Collections The bone collections of the active armature Visible View Layers The view layers of the scene Use for Rendering Custom Any list: set its Collection Data-Path and the Active Item Data-Path Your choice In Live Mode: Click a row to make it the active item. Each click is one undo step. Click a toggle at the end of a row (an eye, a lock...) to flip it on that item. Double-click a row to rename the item. For a material slot, this renames its material. Scroll with the mouse wheel when the rows don't fit. A thin scrollbar shows where you are. Click + to add an item, or − to remove the active one. Only the ready-made lists have these buttons. Settings in the sidebar: Row Toggles: the true / false properties drawn on each row, separated by commas, for example hide, lock. Row Icon: the icon before each name. Clear it, or turn it off, for names only. Reverse Order: lists the last item first. Row Height and Add / Remove. Like other widgets, the list follows the active object. To show one object's list whatever is active, pin it (see Binding Properties). Tip: For a Custom list, the active item path can be a number (active_object.active_material_index) or the item itself (active_object.data.layers.active).

Drag a slider in Live Mode to change a number. When you release, the change is one undo step, and it is keyed if Blender's Auto Keying is on (see Binding Properties). Lineal: a bar. Press it and drag along it: the mouse position sets the value between Min and Max. Hold Shift while dragging to move 10 times finer from where the value is (it never jumps, also when you let go of Shift). Hold Ctrl while dragging to snap to the property's step (1 degree for an angle). Ctrl + click, or double-click, the bar to type the exact value, as in a Number Field. Press Enter to apply it. A typed value is limited by the property only, not by the slider's Min and Max. Radial: a knob. Drag right or up to increase. Shift is 10 times finer, Ctrl snaps to steps (5 degrees for an angle). Lineal 2D: a pad that drives two properties at once, one per axis (each axis has its own Data Path and range). Great for eyes, jaws or facial controls. Look: Eyes draws it as two eyes that look where the value points: a gaze control (see The Armature Picker > Gaze control). In the Slider panel: Unit Type: Value or Angle (the range in degrees), with its Min and Max. Show Value: draws the current value while you drag.

A Number Field shows a number as Blender's own fields do: the value in the middle, with its unit (metres, degrees...) in the scene's unit system, and small arrows on the sides. Its Data Path points to an integer or a float (for example active_object.location[0] or scene.frame_current). A component like active_object.location.x works too: it is the same as location[0]. It is in the Add menu under Sliders. In Live Mode: Drag left or right to change the value. Shift is 10 times finer, Ctrl snaps to the step. Large values move faster. Click an arrow to step the value down or up. Click the field (without dragging) to type the exact value. Press Enter to apply it. Tip: Clicking opens Blender's own field, so you can type an expression or a unit (1.5 m, 90, 10/4). A drag, an arrow click or a typed value is one undo step, and it is keyed if Blender's Auto Keying is on. Note: The widget has no minimum or maximum of its own: only the property's limits apply. In the sidebar: Step: your own step for the arrows and Ctrl, in degrees for an angle. Off: the property's. Precision: decimals shown. Off: the property's. Show Arrows. The Label goes Inside the field by default, on the left of the value, or beside it.

Text on the canvas. Source is: Text: what you type. Property: a property's value, always up to date (a frame number, an object name, on / off, a count...). For a property: Format (Auto, Number, Percent, Yes / No, Identifier), Precision, Units (writes metres, degrees, seconds... in the scene's unit system), Prefix and Suffix.
Shows a picture: open or pick one in the Widget Properties panel. Scale sizes the widget from the image size and keeps its aspect ratio. Fit Image Aspect fixes a widget that was stretched.

Each Image has its own look, in the Image Look section under the image: Opacity: how see-through it is, as you see it on a dark or a light canvas alike (on top of the theme's Image opacity). Saturation: 0 is grey, 1 the image's own colours, up to 2 for more vivid ones. Brightness: 1 as it is; lower is darker, higher is brighter. Tint Amount, Tint and Mode: colour the image. Colorize gives it the tint's colour at its own lightness (a duotone: its lightest parts go towards white), Multiply multiplies it by the tint. A Tint Amount of 0 leaves it as it is.

Turn on Backdrop to put the image behind everything: it draws below every other widget, Frames included. In Live Mode nothing hovers it, it shows no tooltip and clicks go through it to the widgets above. Turn Backdrop off to put a picture on top of a Frame. Inside a Group or a Flex Box a backdrop stays with its container: it draws below the other widgets of that container, not below the rest of the canvas. Keep a backdrop outside containers to have it behind everything. Lock (next to Backdrop, the same as the Transform panel's lock) keeps it from being moved by accident while you edit the widgets on top of it. A click still selects it, and a drag that starts on a locked backdrop draws a selection box, as on empty space. A box selects a backdrop only when it holds all of it, like a Frame. Add > Graphics > Backdrop Image adds one ready to go: Backdrop on, 35 % opacity, no colour. Until you open a picture, it shows a faded placeholder. Open your picture in it and resize it.

A live 3D view on the canvas: a close-up of the object you are working on, what the camera sees, or a second look at your viewport. It updates as you work. Add > Graphics > 3D Views has four ready-made entries. They are all the same widget, set up differently, and you can change any of them later: View Preview: frames the active object. Camera View: what the scene camera sees, inside its frame. Viewport Mirror: follows your 3D Viewport. Silhouette: the flat shape of the active object, seen from the front.

Pick the Source in the sidebar, Widget tab, Source section. Target frames objects for you and keeps them framed when they move or change: Active Object, Selected Objects, an Object you pick (the active object while none is set), or a Collection (its child collections included). Only objects visible in the view layer count. Lights, empties and cameras count as a point. It is a real view of the scene: other objects near the target show too. For the target alone, use Silhouette with Target Only. View: Front, Back, Left, Right, Top, Bottom, or Custom, set with Yaw and Pitch (a three-quarter view at first). Local Axes turns the view with the object when the target is one object. Projection (Perspective or Orthographic), Focal Length, Padding (the room around the objects) and Zoom. Auto Frame frames the target again whenever it moves or changes. Turn it off to keep the framing where it is; Frame sets it again. Camera shows what a camera sees: the Scene Camera (it follows camera markers) or a Camera Object you pick. The camera's frame keeps the render's aspect ratio inside the widget. With Passepartout on, what is outside the frame shows darkened (Alpha sets how much); off, the widget shows bars around the frame. Navigate has two modes: Follow Viewport mirrors a 3D Viewport's view as you navigate. Viewport 0 follows the largest one; 1, 2... a given one (the sidebar says which one, out of how many). A viewport looking through its camera shows the camera's frame. Free Orbit is a view of its own. It starts from the viewport's view (a three-quarter view when the viewport looks straight down an axis). From Viewport copies the chosen viewport's view exactly; Frame Selected frames the selection, else everything. In Live Mode, a Target or Free Orbit preview with Interactive on can be moved with the mouse. Interactive is off for a new Target preview, so the wheel keeps zooming the canvas, and on for a new Free Orbit: drag: orbit; Shift drag: pan (Free Orbit); Ctrl drag or the mouse wheel: zoom; double-click: Free Orbit frames the selection (else everything); a Target goes back to zoom 1. Each drag is one undo step; Esc or a right-click while dragging puts the view back. Camera and Follow Viewport previews don't react to the mouse: the wheel zooms the canvas as usual.

Shading: Solid, Wireframe, Material Preview, or Viewport (the viewport's own shading). Material Preview is heavier: it shows EEVEE's first, noisier sample, and the first time it compiles shaders, which takes a moment. Overlays draws the viewport's overlays (grid, outlines...). Transparent leaves out the world background: the canvas shows through. While you sculpt or paint, a preview uses the viewport's shading whenever Material Preview or Rendered is involved (the sidebar says so): switching shading there would make Blender update the mesh again and again.

Turn on Silhouette to show the flat shape in one colour, as an artist checks a pose or a design. Scope: All Visible is everything the view shows, other objects included. Target Only is only the target objects (with a Camera or Navigate source, pick them in the same section), drawn by the widget itself: it works with no 3D Viewport open. A very heavy target (over 2 million triangles) uses All Visible instead. Color, Background (off: transparent) and Background Color. Outline: Outer draws a line around the shape, Inner along its edge, inside it. Width and Outline Color set it. Changing these colours or the outline is instant: the view is not drawn again.

A preview draws its view again only when something it shows changes: the scene, the camera, the followed viewport, its own settings or its size on screen. Otherwise it costs nothing, however many times the canvas redraws. Off-screen previews draw nothing until you scroll back to them, and the same canvas open in two editors at the same zoom draws its previews once. Max FPS limits how often it draws again while things change (24 by default, 0 for no limit). Live Update off: it changes only when you change one of its settings or click Refresh. Good for a heavy scene. Quality draws more pixels (1.5x, 2x) for smoother edges; Max Size caps the size of the view, in pixels per side.

A preview needs an open 3D Viewport to draw with (a Target silhouette doesn't). Without one it says Open a 3D Viewport. Another window showing the same scene works too. It shows what that viewport shows: its local view, its collection visibility and its clipping. It shows nothing when Blender runs without a window (background mode).

A titled area that holds widgets, like a frame in Blender's node editors. Moving the frame moves what is inside. Drop a widget onto a frame to put it in. Drag it out to take it out. Ctrl J frames the selected widgets, Alt P takes them out. Settings: Title, Title Size, a custom colour, and Shrink (the frame fits its contents; resizing the frame turns it off). Shape: a rounded Rectangle, or a Circle around its contents. A circle frame stays round: resized, it stays square. The checkbox next to Title shows or hides the title. A frame with no title keeps no room for it, so it hugs its contents.

Lines up its children automatically, like a row or a column of a web page. Add a Horizontal Box or a Vertical Box, then drag widgets onto it. Drag a child to reorder it, or out of the box to take it out. Settings: Direction, Wrap and Lines, Justify (where the free space goes), Align (across), Padding and Gap. Each child has a Flex Item panel: Grow, Shrink, Basis, Align Self and fixed sizes. Tip: Hold Alt while dropping a widget on a box to not put it in.
Widgets that move, rotate and resize as one, with no graphic. Select widgets and press Ctrl G. Double-click a group to work inside it, Esc to leave it. Alt G ungroups. See Editing Tools.

Button: a button that selects its bone. Its label is the bone name unless you type another. Button Image: the same with an image. Geometry Shape: a button with any flat shape. Pick a shape in the Custom Shape panel (built-in shapes, your library or the canvas), or make them from meshes with Utils > Import Geo Collection. Hitbox Precision: Convex (fast) or Precise (exact outline). Each bone picker can show an IK/FK puck: a small round switch at its edge that flips the limb between IK and FK. Set it in the IK/FK row of the Widget Properties panel. Tip: See Picker with Rigify for the one-click setup.

Widget What it does Modes Where in the Add menu Example Color Picker Edits a colour right on the canvas All Next to the Color Swatch Color Palette A grid of colour swatches, click one to use it All Next to the Color Picker Brush Picker Makes one brush the active brush Brush modes Under Action Buttons Ring Menu Brushes, toggles and operators in two rings All Under Action Buttons

A Color Picker edits a colour right on the canvas. Its Data Path points to a colour property, like the Color Swatch: a light, the world, a material's Base Color or viewport colour. It shows: a hue and saturation wheel with a brightness bar beside it, an old / new swatch strip, sliders. In the sidebar, Show picks the parts: Wheel, RGB, HSV and Alpha (alpha only for colours with 4 items). By default the wheel and HSV are on and RGB is off.

Shape picks how the colour area looks: Wheel: the hue and saturation wheel with the brightness bar. New pickers and old files use it. Ring + Square: a hue ring around a square, as in Krita or Photoshop. Drag on the ring to change the hue. Drag in the square to set the saturation (left to right) and the brightness (bottom to top).

Drag any part in Live Mode. The colour changes live. When you release, the change is one undo step, and it is keyed if Auto Keying is on. Press Esc or right-click during a drag to put the colour back. The swatch strip shows the colour from the start of the last drag on the left. Tip: From Property still adds a Color Swatch for colour properties. Add a Color Picker from the Add menu, next to the Color Swatch.

The wheel and the HSV sliders work in display space, as Blender's own picker does. The RGB sliders show the stored values (scene linear for most colours), like Blender's R, G and B fields. Bright (HDR) colours above 1 are kept. The V and R, G, B sliders then run from 0 to the value at the start of the drag. The brightness bar stops at 1. Negative channels are kept when you edit other values.

A Color Palette is a grid of colour swatches. Its Data Path points to a colour property, like the Color Picker: the Texture Paint colour, a brush colour, a light or a material colour. Click a swatch in Live Mode and the property gets that colour. The click is one undo step, and it is keyed if Auto Keying is on. A colour with alpha keeps its alpha. Add a Color Palette from the Add menu, next to the Color Picker.

Pick one of two Sources: Own Colors: a list kept in the widget. A new palette starts with twelve colours. Palette: a Blender palette, the same kind Texture Paint uses. Pick it or make a new one in the sidebar. The sidebar lists the swatches: Change a colour there, move it up or down with the arrows, or remove it with the cross. Add Current Color adds the colour the property has now. Note: With a Blender palette, these edits change that palette.

Columns: how many swatches go in a row. The swatches grow to fill the widget. Swatch Size: a largest size for them (0 means fit the widget). Swatch Roundness: rounds their corners. Show Active: rings the swatch that matches the current colour. Add Button: puts a plus button after the swatches. A click on it adds the current colour, like Add Current Color. Note: Swatches are display colours, as in Blender's palettes. A scene linear property gets the matching linear value.

A Brush Picker is one brush on the canvas. Click it in Live Mode and that brush becomes the active brush, as when you pick it in the tool shelf or the asset shelf. A click is one undo step. It works in the modes that use brushes: Sculpt, Vertex Paint, Weight Paint, Texture Paint and Sculpt Curves, the Grease Pencil Draw, Sculpt, Weight and Vertex modes. Find it in the Add menu under Action Buttons. When the active page is set to another mode, it is greyed out there. The Armature Picker has none, since it always works in Pose Mode.

In the sidebar, Choose Brush searches the brush assets: the Essentials that come with Blender, the brushes marked as assets in this file, your own asset libraries. The list shows the brushes of the active page's mode, or of the mode Blender is in. Tip: The eyedropper button, Use Active Brush, stores the brush you are using now. A Brush Picker added while you paint starts with that brush.

Display picks what the widget shows: the icon and the name, only the icon, or only the name. Roundness gives the button its own corners. Turn on the checkbox next to it, then: 0 is a square button, 1 is fully round. A square widget showing only the icon, at 1, is a round brush button. The brush preview is cut to the same shape. Off, the button keeps the theme's corners. Tip: Put round brush buttons in a Frame set to Circle for a small round palette of favourite brushes. Note: The icon is the brush preview, even for a brush not used yet: it is read from the asset file, like the asset shelf does, without adding the brush to your file. The previews are kept in a cache with the date and size of the library file they came from, so they are read again only when that library changes.

The active brush is highlighted. In a mode that can't use the brush, the widget is dimmed and shows an amber mark. If the brush asset can't be found any more (a library was removed or renamed), the widget says "missing" and a click tells you why instead of failing.

A Ring Menu puts brushes, toggles and operators in a ring on the canvas, like a sculpt wheel. It stays on the canvas: it is not a pie menu that opens and closes. It has three parts: The outer ring: round slots. A brush slot shows the brush preview. The inner ring: segments, as many as it has items. The core in the middle: the name of the item under the mouse, or of the active brush. In Live Mode: Click a brush and it becomes the active brush. The active brush has the accent ring. Click a toggle and it switches on or off. A toggle that is on has the accent colour. Click an operator and it runs, here or in a 3D Viewport where it can. Each click is one undo step.

Each item has a Type: Type What a click does What to set Brush Makes the brush active Choose Brush, or the eyedropper for the brush you use now Toggle Switches an on / off property Property: its path, for example tool_settings.sculpt.mesh_automasking_settings.use_automasking_topology Operator Runs an operator Operator, for example paint.mask_flood_fill, and its Arguments, for example mode='INVERT'. On When (optional): a property, for example sculpt_object.use_dynamic_topology_sculpting; while it is on, the item is drawn pressed. Dyntopo uses that one when it is empty A toggle or an operator can also have a Disabled When property: while it is on, the item is greyed out and a click does nothing. For example, Voxel Remesh is disabled while Dyntopo is on (sculpt_object.use_dynamic_topology_sculpting, its default when the field is empty).

The sidebar follows the ring, top to bottom: Page 1 of N: the arrows go to the previous and next page (they wrap around). + adds an empty page after the one shown; the bin removes it, and its brushes (it asks first). Pages only change the outer ring. Outer Ring: the brushes of the page shown. + searches the brush assets and adds one. The brushes button fills the outer ring with every Essentials brush of the canvas page's mode, starting at the ring page shown and going on to new ring pages as needed. Inner Ring: the actions. They are the same on every page. + opens the presets: symmetry, automasking, mask and face sets, Dyntopo, Voxel Remesh, undo and redo, or a custom toggle or operator. The selected item: The arrows move it earlier or later in its ring. You can also duplicate or remove it. Its settings: what it does (see the table), Use a Preset... for an action, its Label in the core and its Icon (a name from the icon packs, for example phosphor:eraser). Page moves a brush to another page, and Ring moves the item to the other ring. Ring Look: how the ring is drawn (see below). In Edit Mode, the selected item has an accent outline on the ring.

Pages hold more brushes: each page has its own outer ring, and the inner ring stays the same. When the ring has more than one page, a tab under it shows the page, for example 1 / 3. Click the arrows on the tab to go back or forward. A click in the middle goes forward. Or turn the mouse wheel over the tab or the core in the middle. Over the rest of the ring the wheel zooms the canvas as usual.

Outer Slots is how many slots the outer ring has at least. Empty slots are drawn faded. Outer Ring and Inner Ring set how wide each ring is. Slot Roundness: 1 for round slots, 0 for square ones. Name in the Core turns the name in the middle on or off. Tip: The Sculpt Wheel demo has a Ring Menu with every sculpt brush, ready to try (see Demo Files).
Everything on this page happens in Edit Mode (Tab).

Click a widget to select it. Shift click adds it to the selection. Shift click the active one to deselect it. Drag on empty space to box select. Click empty space to deselect all. A selects all. Note: A locked widget (the lock in its Transform panel) can be selected but not moved.

Drag a widget to move it. G moves the selection, R rotates it, S scales it, Alt R clears the rotation. The arrow keys nudge by 10 units, Shift + arrow by 1. The handles around the selection resize it (edges and corners) and rotate it (the round knob). Hold Alt to show the pivot and drag it. While you transform, the status bar lists the keys. The main ones: X / Y lock an axis. Shift keeps or frees the aspect ratio (resize), snaps to 15 degrees (rotate) or is finer (scale). Alt resizes from the centre. Ctrl snaps or, with smart snapping on, drags free. Type a number for an exact value. Enter confirms, Esc or right-click cancels. Tip: Exact numbers live in the sidebar, Widget tab, Transform panel.

The magnet in the header turns snapping on or off for this canvas. Its arrow opens the settings: Snap To: edges, centres, spacing (equal gaps) and the grid (with its Grid Size). Snap Distance and Show Guides (the lines that show what you snapped to). Tip: Hold Ctrl while dragging to do the opposite of the current setting.

Shift D duplicates and moves the copy. A group or Flex Box is duplicated with what is inside it, a frame with its widgets. Ctrl C copies the selected widgets, with the same rule. Ctrl V pastes them under the mouse, on the active page, and you move them like after Shift D. A click places them, Esc leaves them under the mouse. X or Delete deletes. Copy and Paste are also in the Selection menu and the right-click menu. Paste from the right-click menu puts the widgets where you right-clicked; from the Selection menu, in the middle of the view. Once something is copied, a right-click with nothing selected opens a menu with just Paste. The status bar says how many widgets were copied or pasted, or why nothing was copied. What you copy stays copied until you copy again: Paste as many times as you like. Each paste is a new copy with its own settings, operator arguments included. A Script button is pasted with its script as it was when you copied it, in a new text of its own. Paste into another canvas of the same kind: Flex Space widgets go into Flex Space canvases, picker widgets into picker canvases. The status bar says when the kinds don't match. The copy is kept even if you delete the original widgets or open another file. A widget copied without its group, Flex Box or frame is pasted on its own. Ctrl Z undoes a paste in one step. Note: Deleting a frame keeps its widgets. Deleting a group deletes what is inside.

A group moves, rotates and resizes several widgets as one. It has no graphic of its own. Ctrl G groups the selection, Alt G ungroups it. Double-click a group to enter it and select one of its widgets. Double-click again to go into a group inside it. Esc or a click outside leaves the group. Ctrl click picks one widget inside a group without entering it first. Shift A inside an open group adds the new widget to that group.

A frame is a titled area that owns the widgets in it: moving it moves them. Ctrl J frames the selection. Alt P removes widgets from their frame. Drop a widget inside a frame to add it. With Shrink on, the frame fits its contents.

With two or more widgets (or a group) selected, a bar appears at the bottom of the canvas: Align left, centre, right, top, middle, bottom, and Align To (the selection bounds, the active widget or the canvas origin). Distribute horizontally or vertically. Size: match or normalize sizes. Group and Ungroup, and More for the rest of the Selection menu. Good to know: Hover a button to see what it does, and why a greyed one can't. The bar moves to the top when the selection is under it. Choose where it shows, or turn it off, in View > Selection Bar (also in the add-on preferences). The same tools are in the header Selection menu and the right-click menu, with Order (bring forward, send back) and Match Rotation.
Right-click a selection for the context menu: frames, Flex Box, groups, order and Delete.

The picture button in the header shows the minimap, a small map of the whole canvas. Its arrow sets when it shows (Edit Mode, Live Mode), its Corner, its Size and whether it draws the widgets. Click the map to centre the view there, drag to pan. Double-click frames every widget, the wheel zooms. Drag its corner grips to move it to another corner or resize it.

The theme sets the colours, shapes and type of every widget, on every canvas. Pick a theme from View > Theme in the header. The same menu has Appearance (Auto follows Blender's theme, Dark, Light), Edit Themes... and Reload Library. Text drawn straight on the canvas (labels, frame titles) always follows the editor's background, so it stays readable when you force Dark or Light against it. A page tab that doesn't fit the current mode is dimmed, but never so much that you can't read it. To make your own theme: Open Edit Themes... (the Themes section of the add-on preferences). Make a New Theme (a copy of Default) or Duplicate the active one. Change it. Note: Built-in themes have a lock. Your themes are saved as files in the theme library folder, so they survive updates. Tip: One widget can keep its own look. In its Style panel, turn on Override Theme. Reset to Theme brings it back.
Sliders, toggles and property labels control a Blender property through a Data Path. Operator buttons run an operator. This page shows the quick ways to set them up.

A data path starts from the current context, the same way Python reaches it through bpy.context: scene.frame_current: the current frame. active_object.location[0]: the X location of the active object. active_object.pose.bones["jaw"]["open"]: a custom property of the bone jaw of the active rig. space_data.overlay.show_overlays: a setting of the editor the widget is drawn in. A path that starts with active_object follows whatever object is active, unless the widget is pinned to one object (see below). Each widget expects one kind of property: sliders and number fields take a number (integer or float), toggles a boolean, an Enum (or a toggle in Set Value mode) an enum or an integer, a Color Swatch, Color Picker or Color Palette a colour, labels anything.

The fastest way to bind a widget: Select the widget in Edit Mode and find its Data Path field in the sidebar. Click the eyedropper button next to the field. The field now says what to pick: Right Click a Slider-Like Property for a slider or number field. Right Click a Boolean Property for a toggle. Right Click an Enum or Integer Property for an Enum (or a toggle in Set Value mode). Right Click a Color Property for a Color Swatch, Color Picker or Color Palette. Right-click the property you want, in any editor (the Properties editor, the sidebar of the 3D Viewport...). Done: the path is filled in for you. For a slider, Min and Max are also set from the property's range. Press Esc to cancel at any time. Tip: For an Operator button, use Pick Operator from UI instead and right-click a button: the operator and its settings are copied.

You don't have to open a canvas first. Right-click any property or button in Blender (the Properties editor, a sidebar, a menu item, a node) and choose Add to FlexSpace Canvas: Right-click the property, for example Location X in the Object properties, or an operator button such as Shade Smooth. Choose Add to FlexSpace Canvas. Its submenu lists your Flex Space canvases: first, the canvas you used last, with its current page (Lights › Main); then its other pages and your other canvases (with many pages, only each canvas' current page); last, New Canvas..., which asks for a name and makes one. Pick a canvas and page. The widget is added there, already set up. What you get is the same as Widgets > Add from Property: a Toggle for an on / off property, an Enum, a slider for a 0–1 range, a Number Field, a Color Swatch, a readout Label for anything else, labelled and bound. A property of an object is pinned to that object. An operator button becomes an Operator button that runs the same operator with the same settings (like Blender's Add to Quick Favorites). On one item of a vector (Location X, a colour's red), the menu has Add All to FlexSpace Canvas (the whole vector, one field per value in a Flex Box) and Add Single to FlexSpace Canvas (only that value, for example active_object.location[0]). The widget goes to a free spot in the part of the page you can see, clear of the other widgets. If there is no room, it goes under them. The page you chose becomes the canvas' current page. The new widget is selected and flashes once. If no editor shows that canvas, Blender's status bar says where it went (Added to Lights › Main). One Ctrl Z removes it. Armature Picker canvases are not listed: add picker widgets from the picker itself. Note: The entry is greyed out when the property can't stay bound: the settings of an operator in its Adjust Last Operation panel or a popup (they only exist while the operator runs), or a property with no data path a canvas can follow. Hover it to see why.

entries.h: Follow the active object or pin one
entries.t: A path that starts with active_object (active_object.data.energy, the power of a light) can work two ways. The pin control under the Data Path field shows which one: Active Object: the widget drives whatever object is active. Select another light and it drives that one. Pinned (the object's name, with a pin icon): the widget always drives that object, whatever is active. Renaming the object keeps the binding. Click the pin control to switch: pinning takes the object that is active now, unpinning makes the widget follow the active object again. The object field next to it pins any other object. On a FlexSpace canvas, the eyedropper and Add from Property pin the object you picked from, so a control panel keeps driving "this light's power". Unpin a widget that should follow the active object. On an Armature Picker, they leave the widget following the active object, so a picker drives whichever rig you are posing. Pin a widget that should always drive one object. Note: If a pinned object is deleted, the widget shows Pinned object is gone. Pin another object, or unpin it to follow the active object. Until then the deleted object stays in the file, kept by the pin, so undo or a re-link into the scene brings the binding back.

Right-click any property in Blender and choose Copy Full Data Path (or hover it and press Ctrl Shift Alt C), then paste it into the Data Path field with Ctrl V. A path like bpy.data.objects["Cube"].location is turned into the form FlexSpace stores, blend_data.objects["Cube"].location. It always drives that object, whatever is active. Note: Copy Data Path (without "Full") gives only the end of the path, like location, which doesn't say whose location. Use Copy Full Data Path.

In Edit Mode a widget whose path doesn't work gets a dashed warning outline and a note in its badge. The sidebar says why under the field: Pick a property, or paste its path (muted): nothing is bound yet. Path not found: the path doesn't lead anywhere (a renamed object or bone, a typo). Pinned object is gone: the object the widget is pinned to was deleted. Not a number, Not a boolean, Not an enum or integer or Not a colour: the property is of the wrong kind for this widget. No items: an Enum bound to an integer has no item list yet (and no small range to show). The canvas top bar counts them on every page that works in the current mode and with the active object (⚠ 2 broken, 1 unbound). Click the count to jump to the next broken widget, see The canvas top bar.

entries.h: Show, hide or disable a widget with a property
entries.t: Any widget can follow a boolean property: show it only while Simplify is on, grey a slider out while the rig is in FK. Select the widget in Edit Mode and open the Conditions panel of the sidebar (Widget tab): Visible When: the widget is shown only while this property is on. In Live Mode a hidden widget is not drawn, can't be clicked, and is left out of the minimap. In Edit Mode it is drawn faint, so you can still select, move and edit it. Disabled When: the widget is greyed out while this property is on (faded by the theme's Disabled Opacity). In Live Mode a click or drag on it does nothing and adds no undo step. Each one takes a data path to a boolean, like a toggle's (for example scene.render.use_simplify). Type or paste it, or use the eyedropper button and right-click a checkbox anywhere in Blender. The arrows button next to the field (Invert) flips it: shown or disabled while the property is off. Under the field the panel says what the condition does now (Shown now, Hidden now, Disabled now, Usable now). A path that doesn't lead to a boolean has no effect (the widget stays shown and usable) and is marked in red. To pick one item of a checkbox row (for example the Z of an object's Lock Location), right-click that checkbox: the path gets its index, like active_object.lock_location[2]. A path that starts with active_object follows the widget's pin, like its data path: a pinned widget reads the condition from its pinned object.

entries.h: Conditions on frames, Flex Boxes and groups
entries.t: A condition on a Frame, a Flex Box or a group applies to every widget inside it too: hide a frame and its members hide with it, disable a Flex Box and all its children are disabled. A widget inside keeps its own conditions as well; it is hidden if it or anything around it is hidden, and disabled the same way. The panel of a widget inside lists what it also follows. Note: A hidden child of a Flex Box keeps its place in the box, so the row shows an empty slot. To close the gap, put the widgets that come and go at the end of the box, or in a box of their own. Note: A condition never changes the widget itself. Pages still decide which widgets are shown at all; a condition only hides or disables a widget that its page shows.

Values are shown the way Blender shows them: Sliders show their value with the property's unit, in the scene's unit system (metres or feet, degrees for rotations). A slider's Unit Type set to Angle lets you type its range in degrees. A property label has a Units option, a Format and a Precision.

A bound widget shows its property's animation state in Blender's own colours (Preferences > Themes > User Interface > State), like Blender's buttons: Green: animated, no keyframe on this frame. Yellow: a keyframe on the current frame. Purple: driven by a driver. Orange: animated, but changed since (not keyed yet). Sliders and knobs tint their track, toggles, enums and number fields their body, a 2D slider its pad, a Color Swatch, a Color Picker and a Color Palette their border and a property label its text. An array item (location[0]) shows its own channel; a widget bound to a whole array (a colour) shows any of its channels. A pinned widget shows the state of its pinned object's property, whatever object is active. In Live Mode (Pose Mode on a picker), with the mouse over the widget: I inserts a keyframe on its property (with your keyframing preferences: Only Insert Needed, visual and cycle-aware keying, the keyframe type). Alt I deletes the keyframe on the current frame, Shift Alt I clears all its keyframes. Backspace resets it to its default value (a custom property: the default of its settings). Each one is a single undo step. On a pinned widget they act on the pinned object. These are Blender's default keys: they follow your User Interface keymap, as over a Blender button, so Industry Compatible (S, Alt S, Shift Alt S) and keys you change in the Preferences work too. Over a bone button or empty space the same keys are Blender's Pose Mode keys, as before.

When Blender's Auto Keying is on (the record button of the Timeline), the end of a slider or number field drag keys the properties it drives, in the same undo step as the change. A click on an Enum or on a toggle (on / off or Set Value) is keyed the same way, and so is a colour changed in a Color Swatch's picker, when the picker closes. A Color Picker drag is keyed on release, and a click on a Color Palette swatch right away. FlexSpace follows your Auto Keying options: Only Insert Available, Only Insert Needed, Replace mode, visual and cycle-aware keying, the keyframe type and Only Active Keying Set. The IK/FK puck of the picker is keyed the same way when you click it.
A picker is a canvas of buttons that select the bones of a rig. You pose without hunting for bones in the viewport. Like any canvas, it can also hold sliders, toggles, labels and images.

The picker belongs to the armature data, so it travels with the rig, also when the rig is linked or appended. Make another armature active and the editor shows that armature's picker. You can also see and change it in Properties > Object Data (armature) > Picker.

Select your rig and enter Pose Mode (Ctrl Tab in the 3D Viewport). Set an area to Armature Picker (Editor Type menu). Click New Picker on the card in the middle. Select some bones in the 3D Viewport and click Import Selected Bones on the card. The picker switches to Edit Mode: click to place each button. The left and right bones of a pair come together. Right-click or Esc cancels the import. Press Tab to go back to posing. Tip: Using Rigify? A full Humanoid Body picker (body, hands, feet and face) takes one step. See Picker with Rigify.

entries.h: When the picker shows a card
entries.t: The picker only works on its own armature, in Pose Mode. Otherwise it shows a card that says why, with a button to fix it: No armature selected or Select an armature: make the rig active. The card offers Pose "rig name" when it can tell which rig uses this picker. Not in Pose Mode: click Enter Pose Mode. "rig name" is linked from another file: a linked rig can't be posed until you make it editable, with Object > Library Override > Make in the 3D Viewport. "rig name" is hidden: show the rig in the view layer to pose it. The picker of "rig name": this editor shows another armature's picker. A picker never poses the wrong rig. Not the picker of ...: no armature uses this picker yet. Click Use it for ... to give it to the active armature.

Click a button: select its bone (the other bones are deselected). Shift click: add the bone to the selection. Shift click the active bone to deselect it. Drag on empty space: box select bones. Click empty space: deselect all. Right-click (with an active bone): the Insert Keyframe pie (Location, Rotation, Scaling, Available). Your Pose Mode keys work here, as if the mouse were in the 3D Viewport: G R S, I, A, Alt A, H, copy and paste pose...

Open the toolbar (T) to pick what a press on a button does: Select & Control (default): select bones and use sliders. Move, Rotate, Scale, Gimball: press a button and drag to transform its bone right away. Release to confirm.
The name of the active bone shows next to its button while you pose. To change this, open the sidebar, Armature tab, Bone Collections panel: Bone Names (Off, Active Bone, Selected Bones).

In the same panel: Sync Bone Collections Visibility hides the buttons of bones whose collections are hidden in the viewport. The armature's bone collections are listed, so you can show and hide them from here. To get a button that shows or hides a collection, add Bone Picker > Bone Collection with Shift A in Edit Mode.

A Lineal 2D pad can be drawn as a pair of eyes: drag anywhere on it and the eyes look that way. The irises follow the value, also when it changes elsewhere (keys, undo, the viewport). In Edit Mode, press Shift A > Data > Numbers > Gaze (Eyes). It comes wide, labelled Gaze, with Look: Eyes. On a Rigify face rig it is bound right away: X and Y move the eye target (eyes, or eye_common on the newer face rigs) left / right and up / down, far enough to turn the eyes about 30 degrees left / right and 15 up / down (further, the irises would roll behind the lids). Any pad can switch: in the sidebar Widget tab, set Look to Pad (the grid and handle) or Eyes. The armature button next to it (Rigify Gaze) binds the pad to the active rig's eye target. The eyes take the pad's style: the whites are the Handle Color, the irises the accent colour, and the pad behind them keeps its colour, so they follow a light or dark canvas. To give the irises a colour of their own (your character's eyes), turn on Override Theme in its Style panel and set Iris Color (with its alpha at 0 they use the accent again). A keyed or animated property tints the pad as usual. In Live Mode an unbound pad shows the eyes without irises (in Edit Mode they look straight ahead, like the Pad handle at the centre). On a dark pad the lashes get a faint light rim. The gaze is relative to the face: X and Y move the eyes right / up as seen from the front of the face, so the pad still works when the head or the whole rig turns. The Face page of Humanoid Body (Rigify) comes with one, already bound, in its Expressions panel, its irises in the face art's eye colour.

Press Tab to edit the picker. The Utils menu in the header has: Import Selected Bones: a button for each bone selected in the viewport that has none yet. Import Geo Collection: turns the flat meshes of a collection into Geometry Shape buttons. A mesh named like a bone is bound to that bone. Repair Bone Bindings: see Picker with Rigify > Repair bindings. Move Selected to Page. To bind a button by hand, select it. Then, in the sidebar Widget tab, either: pick the Bone from the list, or select the bone in the viewport and click the arrow button at the left of the field (Assign Active Bone). A button with no label takes the bone's name. Moving things around works like any canvas, smart snapping included (see Editing Tools > Smart snapping). Note: Buttons follow renamed bones. A button whose bone is gone shows Missing bone and does nothing when clicked.

A picture of the character behind its buttons makes the picker easier to read, and to build. In Edit Mode, Shift A > Graphics > Backdrop Image. Open the picture in the sidebar, Widget tab, then move and resize it under the buttons. Set its look in Image Look: it starts at 35 % opacity and in grey, so the buttons stand out. Raise Saturation to bring its colours back, or use Tint to give it one colour. Turn on Lock so it stays put while you place buttons on top of it. Dragging over a locked backdrop draws a selection box, so you can still select the buttons on it. A backdrop draws below every widget, Frames included, and in Live Mode clicks go through it to the buttons. See Widgets > Image for every option. Tip: The Face page of Humanoid Body (Rigify) is built this way: a face picture as a locked backdrop, with every face control drawn on its feature and a gaze pad drawn as eyes. See Rigify > Bone collections for what is on it.

Buttons of bones named with a side (hand.L, hand_R, Left/Right...) know their other side. In Edit Mode, moving, resizing or rotating one of a pair mirrors the other across the red centre line. Buttons of centre bones stay on the line. A side button can't cross it.
How to build a picker for a rig generated with Rigify. The same ideas work for any rig.

Want a full picker in one step? Select the generated rig. In the picker's Edit Mode, press Shift A. Choose Bone Picker > Humanoid Body (Rigify). The chart comes with its own character drawings: a male and a female body, both hands, both feet and a male and a female face. Every shape is traced from them, so each control sits on the right part of the drawing. Body: Adult Male or Adult Female. Each has its own drawing, and the shapes follow it. Pages: Body, Hands, Feet and Face. Each one goes on its own page, with its own tab, or all four sit side by side on one page with Each on Its Own Page off. Body page: the body split into head, neck, chest, torso, hips, shoulders, arms, hands, legs and feet (the FK and torso controls), plus the IK hands and feet, the elbow and knee poles, the spine and the tweaks. The IK hand (diamond) and its IK/FK switch are past the fingertips, the IK feet beside the feet, the poles and the IK arm and thigh bars just outside the limbs. These markers are exact left/right mirror images, so editing them with mirror on moves both sides together. Hands page: both hands, large: the palm, every finger and thumb segment, the fingertips (past each fingertip, along the finger) and the finger masters (in a row past the fingertips, each under its finger; the thumb's past its tip). The wrist band is the FK hand, with the hand tweak (dot) on it. Next to it: the IK hand (pill) and its IK/FK switch. Feet page: both feet seen from above, large: heel, foot, ball (foot spin) and toe controls, every toe with its tip and master, and the FK foot and toe bars on the outer side. Face page (on by default): every control of Rigify's face on an anime face, the female face for Adult Female and the male face for Adult Male: lids, eye rings and pupils, brows, cheeks, nose, lips, jaw, ears, the EYES and JAW bars, and the teeth and tongue in their own frame. On the left, an Expressions panel: a Gaze pad drawn as two eyes in the face's eye colour, bound to the eye target (drag it and the eyes look there), a pad per mouth corner and the Mouth Lock and Eyes Follow knobs. On the right, the face bone collection toggles, each with a Solo button. See Bone collections below for what each shape is. It works with both Rigify faces: the classic one and the newer one that Upgrade Face Rig makes (eye_common), where the few controls with other names (the eye masters, the mouth corners, the tongue) go to their bones there. A rig without a Rigify face gets no Face page, and a note says so. Scale sets the size of the chart. IK/FK Switches: when on, each arm and leg gets a Rigify IK/FK puck of its own, right next to the IK hand or foot (never on top of it), so both are easy to click. Character Backdrop (on by default): puts each page's drawing behind it as a locked Backdrop Image, at the same scale as the shapes. The drawing is faded and half grey (75 % opacity, 50 % saturation, a light cool tint) and the body shapes are see-through over it, so you see the art and the colours at once. The face keeps more of its colour and its controls stay solid. Clicks go through the drawing to the controls. Change its look in its Image Look section, or delete it. Turn the option off for the shapes alone, solid. Hands Side: Back (the default) or Palm: the drawing of the Hands page, and the shapes follow it.
